Prevention: Do not apply more than recommended nitrogen fertilizer as this will increase leave growth which favours aphid egg laying (Not more than 45kgN per hectare at planting.
Plant and/or maintain habitats that support beneficial insects such as flowers or grass strips.
Such beneficial insects can largely reduce aphid populations.
Dust with ash other plants growing near the strawberries if they are hosting aphids before they enter the strawberry field.
Plant strawberry varieties resistant to viruses transmitted by aphids such as
Andreas which is moderately tolerant to most viral diseases.
Monitoring: Inspect strawberry fields especially when young and during flowering, every 3 to 4 days.
Look under the leaves, especially along main veins particularly at the base of leaves of every 10th plant.
Look for clusters of tiny light- green soft-bodied pear-shaped insects (about 1 to 3 mm long).
Most are wingless, few have wings.
Take action when aphids reach 5 to 10 per leaf on the inspected plants.
It’s too late if the aphids have started attacking the fruits.
Look for sticky honeydew or blackish sooty moulds on fruits and leaves.
If on leaves, action may still be possible.
If many natural enemies, are near the aphid colonies, such as lady beetle adults and their larvae, no action may be needed.
Direct Control: Mix 1 tablespoon of soap (non-perfumed) with 4L of water and spray the crop early in the morning or late afternoon.
Dust ash evenly onto the infested parts of the crop.
Soak green leaves and seeds of castor oil plant for 24 hours in water, filter, dilute and spray.

Release when temperatures are below 30° C.
Pirimicarb at the rate of 7g/20 litres of water.
Restrictions: When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval.

In most cases, no application of synthetic insecticides is needed against aphids in strawberries, because they only do damage in high numbers (see thresholds), and are often controlled by natural enemies.
Note that insecticides will kill most of those natural enemies.
In case of sprays, good coverage is needed, as aphids hide below leaves.
